    GitHub Actions Lab

    Learn GitHub Actions by writing it. An editor checks every line as you type, with the actionlint linter running in your browser, and shows what would run for a push, a pull request, a tag or a merge queue. Write pipelines from nothing, then read broken ones and fix them, until you can build an enterprise CI/CD pipeline without looking anything up.

    00

    What you'll be able to do

    Goal: by the end you can write an enterprise CI/CD pipeline for GitHub Actions from an empty file, and read someone else's pipeline, find what is wrong with it and fix it, without looking up a single command.

    How this lab works

    Reading about pipelines does not teach you to write them. So most of this page is an editor. You are told what to build, you type it, and the page checks it as you type. A line with a mistake turns red with the line number and a plain explanation. A requirement turns green when you meet it. The answer stays out of sight until you ask for it.

    Each lesson lab can start two ways, and you choose: Guided gives you the lesson's starting file and you add the new part, Empty gives you a blank file and you type every line. You do not need to know the keywords first. Under the editor, the page lists the keys that fit on the line your cursor is on, each with what it means, and Ctrl+Space types the first one. When you are stuck, Next line shows only the next line your file needs, and Show solution opens the finished file next to yours. Neither changes what you typed, and you never have to start a lab over to see the answer.

    The checking is done by three things working together: actionlint, the most widely used linter for GitHub Actions workflows (an open-source project, not made by GitHub; version 1.7.12, compiled to WebAssembly so it runs inside this page, and nothing you type leaves your browser); requirement checks written for each exercise (the right trigger, the right permission, the right order); and a run preview that shows which jobs would start for a push, a pull request, a tag or a merge queue, and why.

    PartWhat you doSkill
    Steps 1 to 13: guided labsOne idea per step, a short explanation, then an editor that starts you off, or starts empty if you choose. Easy at the top, expert at the bottom: triggers, jobs, matrix, caches, secrets, images, environments, OIDC, reuse, hardening, governance.Learn the pieces
    Step 14: command drillsType the gh and git commands a pipeline needs. Each answer is checked against the real command's flags.No more googling commands
    Step 15: delivery patternsHow a team splits a pipeline into files, how variables and secrets get in, dev to uat to prod, settings for a .NET API, and deploying a single-page app.Arrange the pieces
    Step 16: write from scratchAn empty editor and a checklist. Twelve challenges from easy to hard, some with several files.Write a pipeline
    Step 17: the capstoneThe enterprise pipeline for the Todo project, with 20 requirements, from nothing.Write an enterprise pipeline
    Step 18: read and fixFourteen broken pipelines with the symptom the team saw, from "invalid workflow file" to a pipeline with seven separate faults.Read a pipeline and fix it
    Step 19: sandboxPaste any workflow of your own and check it.Use it on real work
    Step 20: run it for realPut an exercise in a practice repository on GitHub, trigger it, watch it and read its logs.See it run

    Every example is about the project you build in the other tutorials: a .NET API in src/api, an Angular UI in src/ui, a Docker Hub image, a Helm chart and a cluster. Every action named here is at the version its own repository publishes today, read from GitHub when this page was built.

    What the checker cannot do. It cannot run your workflow, reach GitHub or AWS, or know your repository's settings. To run an exercise on GitHub itself, follow step 20. It checks structure, names, types, expressions and the logic of your conditions. GitHub also validates a file when you push it. Things that live in the repository's settings (rulesets, environment protection rules, secrets) cannot be tested here, and each step says where they are. The actionlint build in the browser leaves out the optional shellcheck and pyflakes checks of your scripts.

    Your lab progress

    This is the route a change takes through GitHub Actions, from git push to a result on the pull request. Play it with the arrows, or let it run:

    Words you will meet

    Workflow
    One YAML file in .github/workflows/. It says when to run and what to run. A repository can have many.
    Event
    What starts a workflow: a push, a pull request, a tag, a schedule, a button, or another workflow.
    Job
    A group of steps that run on one machine. Jobs run in parallel unless one needs another.
    Step
    One command (run) or one action (uses), run in order inside a job.
    Runner
    The machine that runs a job. GitHub-hosted runners are fresh virtual machines; self-hosted runners are your own.
    Action
    A packaged, reusable step written by someone else (or you), such as actions/checkout.
    Context
    An object of facts about the run that you read in ${{ }}: github, runner, env, vars, secrets, needs, matrix, steps, inputs.
    Expression
    A small formula in ${{ }} or in an if: comparisons, &&, ||, and functions like contains().
    Secret and variable
    Stored values. Secrets are encrypted and masked; variables are plain settings.
    Artifact and cache
    An artifact keeps files from a run, for download or for a later job. A cache keeps files (such as packages) so the next run does not download them again.
    Environment
    A named place you deploy to, such as staging. It can require approval and holds its own secrets.
    Matrix
    One job definition run once for every combination of values you list.
    Reusable workflow
    A workflow that other workflows call as a job, with inputs, secrets and outputs.
    OIDC
    OpenID Connect: GitHub gives a job a short-lived signed token, and a cloud exchanges it for temporary credentials, so no long-lived key is stored.
    01

    Your first workflow

    Goal: a workflow that starts on the right events and prints two facts about the run, with no red lines in the editor.

    Why this step

    A workflow is a text file. If you can read the file, you can predict what GitHub will do. This step names the four parts you will see in every file, and the few YAML rules that cause most of the "why does nothing run" problems.

    GitHub looks for workflows in the .github/workflows folder at the root of your repository, in files ending in .yml or .yaml. When something happens, GitHub reads the files as they are in the commit that caused the event. A workflow has these parts:

    YAML rules that bite. Indent with spaces: a tab is an error. A value that contains : (a colon and a space) must be quoted or written as a block: run: echo "Title: x" is invalid, while run: | followed by an indented line is fine. A pattern that starts with *, [ or ! needs quotes. And a version such as 3.10 is the number 3.1 unless you quote it: '3.10'. The editor below reports each of these as you type.

    Wherever you see ${{ … }}, GitHub evaluates the expression and pastes the result into the file before the shell sees it. github and runner are contexts: objects of facts about the run, such as github.repository and runner.os.

    Sources. Workflows, Workflow syntax

    What you just learned

    • A workflow has events, jobs, a runner, and steps. Steps are either run (a command) or uses (an action).
    • Branch filters sit under the event: push: branches: [main].
    • ${{ }} is replaced with a value before the command runs.
    02

    Build and test the .NET API

    Goal: a job that checks out the code, installs .NET 10, restores, builds and tests the Todo API.

    Why this step

    Continuous integration is this job: on every change, build the code and run the tests on a clean machine, so "works on my PC" is not the only evidence. Nearly every pipeline starts with these three moves.

    The runner is empty at the start. actions/checkout downloads your repository onto it. actions/setup-dotnet puts the SDK you ask for on the path. GitHub-hosted runners come with some SDKs installed, but naming the version makes it part of your file: a build today and a build next year use the same SDK.

    An action is written owner/repo@version. The version after the @ is a tag, and each action's own repository decides which tags exist. The versions used on this page were read from each repository: checkout@v7, setup-dotnet@v6. The editor warns you if you use an older major version, or a version that does not exist.

    • uses runs an action. Its inputs go in with:.
    • run runs a shell command. It uses bash on Linux runners.
    • defaults.run.working-directory sets the folder for every run step in a job. It does not apply to uses steps.
    • --no-restore and --no-build let each dotnet command reuse the work of the one before.

    Sources. Building and testing .NET, actions/setup-dotnet

    What you just learned

    • The standard CI job: checkout, setup, then restore, build and test.
    • Actions are versioned. Use the current major version, and read the action's repository for its inputs.
    • The red gutter and the Problems panel are the same rules a linter would apply on your own PC.
    03

    Choose when it runs

    Goal: triggers that start the pipeline for the right branches, tags and files, by hand, and on a schedule, and the filter patterns to match them.

    Why this step

    A trigger that is too wide wastes minutes and hides the runs that matter. One that is too narrow leaves a change unchecked. Most "my workflow did not run" questions are a filter question, and filters have rules worth knowing exactly.

    Events and their filters

    • push has branches, tags, branches-ignore, tags-ignore, paths and paths-ignore. If you list only tags (or only branches), the workflow does not run for the other kind of ref. If you list neither, it runs for both.
    • pull_request filters branches on the target branch, the one you merge into. Its default activity types are opened, synchronize and reopened.
    • workflow_dispatch adds a "Run workflow" button, with typed inputs (string, number, boolean, choice, environment). The file must be on the default branch for the button to show.
    • schedule takes POSIX cron in UTC, runs on the latest commit of the default branch, and the shortest interval is 5 minutes. Runs are delayed when GitHub is busy, which includes the start of each hour. In a public repository, scheduled workflows are disabled after 60 days without repository activity.

    You cannot use branches with branches-ignore, tags with tags-ignore, or paths with paths-ignore for the same event. To include and exclude together, use the include list with ! entries.

    The pattern rules

    PatternMeaningMatches
    *Anything except /feature/* matches feature/login, not feature/a/b
    **Anything, including /feature/** matches feature/a/b/c
    ? and +Zero or one, or one or more, of the character beforev[0-9]+ matches v2 and v210
    [0-9]One character from a class (ranges a-z, A-Z, 0-9 only)v[12].0 matches v1.0, v2.0
    !patternRemoves what the patterns before it matched. A later positive pattern adds it backreleases/** then !releases/**-alpha
    docs/**/*.mdFor paths, **/ may match no folder at allmatches docs/README.md and docs/a/b.md

    Path patterns must match the whole path, from the repository root. Because *, [ and ! are special in YAML, a pattern that starts with one of them must be quoted. Try the drills first. You write the patterns, and the table shows every case at once.

    Filters and required checks. If a workflow is skipped because of a path filter, a branch filter or a [skip ci] commit message, its checks stay pending. A pull request that requires those checks cannot merge. Do not put path filters on a workflow that a ruleset requires (step 13 shows the pattern that avoids this).

    Now write the whole on: block. Use the preview under the editor: it takes the event you pick and tells you whether the workflow would start, and why.

    Sources. Events that trigger workflows, Workflow syntax: filter pattern cheat sheet

    What you just learned

    • Branch and tag filters and path filters are separate, and both must pass when both are present.
    • pull_request filters on the target branch. ** crosses folders, * does not.
    • Skipped by a filter means pending, not passed, which matters for required checks.
    04

    Jobs, conditions and expressions

    Goal: jobs in the right order, a condition that decides whether one runs, and data passed from one job to the next. You can write the condition and the expression yourself.

    Why this step

    A pipeline is a graph of jobs. needs draws the edges, if decides which jobs take part, and outputs carry data along the edges. Conditions are small programs, and they fail silently: a wrong one skips a job without a warning.

    • needs makes a job wait. If a needed job fails or is skipped, the job is skipped too, unless its if contains a status function such as always().
    • A skipped job reports success. It does not stop a pull request from merging, even if it is a required check.
    • Job outputs are how data crosses jobs: a step writes name=value to the file $GITHUB_OUTPUT, the job lists it under outputs, and another job reads needs.<job>.outputs.<name>. A job can read only the jobs it lists in its own needs.
    • Status functions: success() is applied by default. failure(), cancelled(), always(). GitHub recommends !cancelled() over always(), because always() also runs when you cancel the run.

    Expressions

    Inside ${{ }} (or directly in an if) you can use literals, the operators ( ) [ ] . ! < <= > >= == != && ||, and a few functions. Rules worth knowing:

    • Strings use single quotes; double quotes are an error. Comparing strings ignores case, so 'Main' == 'main' is true.
    • Comparing different types converts them to numbers. null is 0, true is 1, an empty string is 0, and text that is not a number is NaN, which is never equal to anything.
    • && and || return one of their values, so a || 'default' works as a default.
    • In an if, false, 0, '' and null are false, and everything else is true. That is why if: "${{ x }} == 'y'" is always true: the text around the braces makes it a non-empty string.
    • contains(), startsWith(), endsWith() ignore case. format(), join(), toJSON(), fromJSON(), hashFiles() and case() are the others, and .* picks a field from every item of a list.

    Where can you use which context? It depends on the key. The if of a job can read only github, needs, vars and inputs: no secrets, no env, no matrix. The if of a step can also read env, steps, job, runner, matrix and strategy, but still not secrets. The checker reports a context used in the wrong place.

    Write six conditions. The table lists the cases your expression must get right.

    Try your own

    Pick an example or write an expression, and change the context as JSON to see the value.

    Sources. Expressions, Contexts and where each is available, Control jobs with conditions, Pass job outputs

    What you just learned

    • needs orders jobs, outputs pass data, and if decides who takes part.
    • An if is an expression: case-insensitive strings, single quotes, && and || that return values.
    • Never mix text and ${{ }} in an if. Use github.ref for the full ref and github.ref_name for the short one.
    05

    One job, many combinations

    Goal: a matrix that runs the tests on several systems and SDKs from one job definition, minus the combinations you do not need.

    Why this step

    Software has to work on more than one thing: a second operating system, the SDK you support next to the one you build with. A matrix turns that into one job definition and a few lists, instead of copying jobs.

    • Every key under matrix is a variable with a list. The job runs once for every combination: os: [a, b] and dotnet: [x, y] make four jobs.
    • exclude removes the combinations that match every key you list.
    • include adds values to the combinations it fits, or adds a new combination if it fits none without changing an original value.
    • A run can have at most 256 matrix jobs.
    • fail-fast defaults to true: one failure cancels the jobs still running or waiting. Set it false to see every failure. max-parallel limits how many run at once. continue-on-error on the job lets one matrix job fail without failing the run.
    • The matrix can come from data: matrix: ${{ fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.matrix) }}.

    Sources. Running variations of jobs, Actions limits

    What you just learned

    • Matrix variables multiply: two lists of two are four jobs. exclude subtracts.
    • matrix.<name> reads the current job's values.
    • Think about fail-fast: it is on by default.
    06

    Caches and artifacts

    Goal: packages restored from a cache instead of downloaded, and a build output kept as an artifact that a later job can download.

    Why this step

    Every job starts on an empty machine, so each run downloads every package again, and the files a job makes disappear when it ends. A cache removes the repeated download. An artifact keeps what you built. They look alike and do different jobs.

    CacheArtifact
    ForThings you can rebuild, to save time: packages, build intermediatesResults you want to keep or pass on: build output, test reports
    Found byA key. An exact match is a hit; restore-keys are prefixes tried nextA name, unique within the run
    If it is missingThe job still works, only slower. A new cache is saved at the end if the job succeededThe job that needs it fails
    LifetimeRemoved after 7 days without use. 10 GB per repository by defaultKept for the retention you set
    Visible toRuns on the same branch, or on the default branchDownloadable from the run page and with gh run download
    • A cache key should change only when the inputs change: hashFiles('**/*.csproj'). A key that includes github.sha never matches an earlier run.
    • actions/setup-dotnet has cache: true, but it needs a packages.lock.json and fails without one. The Todo API has none, so use actions/cache with the project files. actions/setup-node has cache: npm, which uses the package-lock.json.
    • Do not store secrets in a cache: anyone who can open a pull request against the repository can read caches of the base branch.
    • Artifact names must be unique in a run and artifacts cannot be changed once created. In a matrix, put the matrix values in the name.
    • working-directory does not apply to uses: steps, so an action's path starts from the repository root.

    Sources. Dependency caching, actions/upload-artifact, actions/cache

    What you just learned

    • A cache key must repeat when the inputs repeat. hashFiles does that.
    • Artifacts are the way to hand files to a later job, and each name can be used once.
    • Paths in with: are from the repository root.
    07

    Secrets, variables and least privilege

    Goal: a workflow where secrets cannot leak through a script, the automatic token has only the access the job needs, and untrusted text is never run as code.

    Why this step

    A pipeline holds your keys and can write to your repository. It runs code that came from other people's pull requests and from third-party actions. The habits here are the difference between a pipeline and an open door.

    • Secrets (secrets.NAME) are encrypted, and masked in logs. Variables (vars.NAME) are plain text, for settings such as a user name. Both can be set for a repository, an environment, or an organization. gh secret set and gh variable set are in the command drills.
    • Anyone with write access can read every repository secret through a workflow. Secrets are not a defence against your own collaborators, so keep the value's power small.
    • Masking is not guaranteed once a secret is transformed (Base64, URL-encoding, a JSON blob). Do not store structured data as a secret, and register any derived sensitive value with ::add-mask::.
    • The GITHUB_TOKEN is created for each run. Its permissions come from permissions: once you list any scope, every scope you do not list becomes none. A job-level permissions replaces the workflow-level one for that job. read-all, write-all and {} (none) are the shorthands. GitHub's advice is to default the token to read-only for repository contents and raise it per job.
    • Script injection. ${{ }} is replaced before the shell runs, so text written by other people (a pull request title, a branch name, a commit message, an issue body) pasted into run: becomes code. Pass it through env and read the shell variable.
    • Fork pull requests get a read-only token and no secrets. That is why pull_request is safe for untrusted code.

    Sources. Secure use reference, Use GITHUB_TOKEN for authentication

    What you just learned

    • Put secrets and untrusted text in env, never in the script text.
    • Name the permissions you need and nothing else. Raise them on the one job that needs it.
    • secrets are for sensitive values, vars for settings.
    08

    Build and push the image

    Goal: the Docker workflow of the Todo project, with pull requests that build without pushing, tags that are derived for you, and layers cached between runs.

    Why this step

    In the first tutorial you wrote docker build and docker push by hand in a script. The actions published by Docker do the same work, with caching, multiple tags and the right labels, and they make "build on pull requests, publish on merges" a two-line condition.

    • docker/login-action logs in to the registry. Without registry it uses Docker Hub. Store the token as a secret, the user name as a variable.
    • docker/setup-buildx-action prepares the builder that supports caching and multiple platforms.
    • docker/metadata-action computes tags and labels from the event: type=sha gives sha-a1b2c3d (add prefix= for the bare 7 characters), type=ref,event=tag gives the tag name, type=raw,value=… gives a fixed name. Its outputs are tags and labels.
    • docker/build-push-action builds, and pushes when push: true. cache-from: type=gha and cache-to: type=gha,mode=max keep layers in the GitHub Actions cache.
    • Docker Hub limits. GitHub-hosted runners are exempt from Docker Hub's pull rate limit when pulling public images. Pulling private images from Docker Hub is subject to it, and self-hosted runners always are.
    • Never publish a moving tag like latest as the thing you deploy: you cannot tell what is running or roll back. Deploy by commit tag, and later by digest.

    Sources. docker/build-push-action, docker/metadata-action, Publishing Docker images

    What you just learned

    • Build on every pull request, push only on trusted events: one condition used twice.
    • Let metadata-action compute tags and labels, and the Docker cache keep the layers.
    • Tag with the commit, not latest.
    09

    Environments, approvals and concurrency

    Goal: a path from build to staging to production where production waits for approval, deploys never overlap, and a running production deploy is never cancelled.

    Why this step

    Continuous delivery is not "deploy everything instantly". It is a pipeline where each stage has the checks it deserves. GitHub environments hold those rules, and concurrency keeps two deploys from fighting.

    Environments

    An environment is named in the job with environment: production. Its rules are set in the repository under Settings → Environments, not in the YAML:

    • Required reviewers: up to six people or teams; one of them must approve. You can forbid the person who started the deployment from approving it.
    • Wait timer: delay a job by 1 to 43,200 minutes (30 days).
    • Deployment branches and tags: which refs may deploy to it.
    • Environment secrets and variables: available only to jobs that name the environment, and for an environment with reviewers only after approval.

    Check your plan. On GitHub Free, Pro and Team, required reviewers and wait timers on environments are available for public repositories only. Private repositories need a higher plan for them. Environment secrets for private repositories also need a paid plan. The YAML in this step is valid either way, but the gate only holds if your plan supports it.

    Concurrency

    • A concurrency group allows one running job or run at a time. A new one waits as pending, and by default a newer pending run replaces an older pending one.
    • cancel-in-progress: true also cancels the one that is running. It is right for pull request checks and wrong for a deployment.
    • Group names are case-insensitive and can use the github, inputs and vars contexts (at job level also needs, strategy and matrix).
    • Set timeout-minutes on every job. The default is 360 minutes (6 hours), the longest a GitHub-hosted job can run.

    Sources. Deployments and environments, Workflow syntax: concurrency

    What you just learned

    • An environment is a name in the YAML and a set of rules in the settings. The job pauses until the rules are met.
    • Cancel superseded checks, never a running deploy.
    • A timeout is part of every job.
    10

    Keyless access to the cloud

    Goal: a deploy job that reaches AWS with a short-lived identity token, with no access key stored in GitHub.

    Why this step

    A cloud access key kept as a secret never expires, can be copied by anyone who can run a workflow, and is the thing that leaks. OpenID Connect replaces it: GitHub vouches for the job, and the cloud decides whether to trust that statement.

    The subject claim

    The trust policy should accept only the subjects you expect. By default the subject is built from the job:

    The jobSubject, repositories created before 15 July 2026
    uses an environmentrepo:OWNER/REPO:environment:NAME
    runs for a pull request, no environmentrepo:OWNER/REPO:pull_request
    on a branch, no environmentrepo:OWNER/REPO:ref:refs/heads/BRANCH
    on a tag, no environmentrepo:OWNER/REPO:ref:refs/tags/TAG

    Newer repositories use a different form. For repositories created after 15 July 2026, and for repositories renamed or transferred after that date, the default subject includes the numeric owner and repository ids: repo:OWNER@OWNER_ID/REPO@REPO_ID:environment:NAME. A trust policy written in the old form is refused for such a repository. Older repositories keep the old form unless you opt in. Use GitHub's actions-oidc-debugger action to print the claims a run would send before you write the policy.

    Always put at least one condition on sub in the trust policy. Without one, any repository could ask for your role. Using an environment in the job, with deployment branch rules on that environment, makes the subject depend on a protected name.

    Sources. OpenID Connect reference, OIDC in Amazon Web Services, aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials

    What you just learned

    • id-token: write lets a job request an identity token. The cloud's trust policy decides whether to accept it.
    • The subject names the environment, branch, tag or pull request, and in newer repositories the numeric ids.
    • Give id-token: write only to the job that deploys.
    11

    Reuse: workflows and composite actions

    Goal: one build workflow that every service calls, and one composite action that packages a few steps, with typed inputs, secrets and outputs.

    Why this step

    Teams copy a pipeline into every repository, and then fix a bug in one of twelve copies. Two tools remove the copies, and they are not the same thing, so knowing which to use is part of the skill.

    Reusable workflowComposite action
    What it isA whole workflow with on: workflow_call, called as a jobA list of steps in an action.yml, used as a step
    Runs onIts own runners, chosen by its own jobsThe runner of the job that uses it
    Input and outputTyped inputs, secrets, outputs mapped from job outputsInputs and outputs (an output's value is an expression)
    Called withuses: ./.github/workflows/x.yml or owner/repo/.github/workflows/x.yml@refuses: ./.github/actions/x or owner/repo/path@ref
    Use it to shareA pipeline stage, with its own jobs and environmentsA few steps that belong inside a job
    • A calling job has uses, with, secrets (or secrets: inherit), and may have needs and if. It cannot have runs-on, steps or environment. Set the environment on a job inside the called workflow.
    • A workflow output must map to a job output; a job output maps to a step output.
    • A local reference (./.github/workflows/…) is taken from the same commit as the caller. For another repository, pin a tag or a full SHA.
    • Workflows can call workflows up to ten levels deep (the caller plus nine). Permissions through the chain can stay the same or shrink, never grow.
    • Every run step in a composite action needs a shell.

    Write the reusable workflow

    Call it twice

    Package steps as a composite action

    Sources. Reuse workflows, Create a composite action

    What you just learned

    • A reusable workflow is called as a job and brings its own runners; a composite action is steps inside your job.
    • A job can read needs.X.outputs only for jobs it lists in needs.
    • shell is required in composite actions.
    12

    Supply-chain security: pin, scan, sign

    Goal: pinned actions, code and dependency scanning on every change, and an image that is signed and carries proof of how it was built.

    Why this step

    Your pipeline runs other people's code with your secrets, and it ships what it builds to production. Attackers know. Three layers cover most of the risk: control what runs in the pipeline, look for problems before they merge, and prove what you shipped.

    Control what runs

    • Pin to a full commit SHA. A tag can be moved or deleted if the action's repository is compromised. A SHA cannot. Verify the SHA belongs to the action's own repository, not a fork, and keep a # v… comment so Dependabot can update it.
    • Actions with immutable releases publish exact tags (such as dependency-review-action@v5.0.0) that cannot be moved, with no moving v5 tag. An exact version is as strong as it gets without a SHA.
    • GitHub is previewing workflow dependency lockfiles (gh actions-lock), which pin every action including the ones your actions use. It was in preview on GitHub Enterprise Cloud when this page was written.
    • Untrusted checkouts. pull_request_target and workflow_run run with secrets and a writable token. Never build or run code from a pull request's head in them (a "pwn request"). actions/checkout refuses a fork's head ref in pull_request_target unless you set allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true. GitHub also adds a default policy that blocks pull_request_target in public repositories, enforced from 2 November 2026 for repositories that were on the default policy.
    • persist-credentials: false on checkout keeps the token out of the repository's git config for a build that never pushes.

    Look for problems

    CodeQL scans source code for vulnerabilities and uploads the findings to the Security tab. Dependency review compares the dependencies of a pull request with the base and fails when it introduces a vulnerable package. Code scanning is free for public repositories. Dependency review works on public repositories, and on private ones with GitHub Advanced Security.

    Prove what you shipped

    Sign the image by digest (a tag can move, a digest cannot) with cosign, keyless, so the signature is tied to this workflow's identity and nothing is stored. Create a build provenance attestation with actions/attest: signed facts about which repository, workflow and commit built a digest. Check it later with gh attestation verify. In part 4 of the Todo series a Kyverno policy refuses an unsigned image from entering the cluster. This is the pipeline half of that.

    Plans. Artifact attestations are available for public repositories on every plan. For private repositories on Free, Pro and Team they need GitHub Enterprise Cloud. Cosign signing works on any plan.

    Sources. Secure use reference, Securely using pull_request_target, Artifact attestations

    What you just learned

    • Pin by SHA (or exact immutable tag), and let Dependabot update the pin.
    • Never run a pull request's code in a privileged trigger.
    • Scan on every pull request, sign by digest, and attest what you built.
    13

    Governance: keep the pipeline honest

    Goal: dependencies that update themselves, one stable required check that works with a merge queue, and the right people reviewing the pipeline files.

    Why this step

    A good pipeline file means little if anyone can change it unreviewed, if it quietly falls out of date, or if the merge rules depend on job names that change. The last layer is a handful of files and settings around the workflow.

    • Dependabot opens pull requests for outdated dependencies, including the actions in your workflows, NuGet and npm packages, Docker base images, Helm charts and Terraform. Updates wait a default 3 days after a release (a cooldown), and you can lengthen that. Security updates are never delayed.
    • Rulesets (Settings → Rules) can require status checks, pull request reviews and review from code owners before merging, and a merge queue. These are settings, not YAML, so you cannot test them here.
    • A required check is a name. If you require api and ui by name, renaming or adding a job breaks the rule, and a skipped job reports success. Require one gate job that always runs and fails if anything failed.
    • Merge queue. A queued pull request is built together with the latest main and the changes ahead of it. It starts workflows with the merge_group event, so every required workflow must listen for it, or the check never reports and the pull request never merges.
    • CODEOWNERS asks the right team to review files they own. The last matching line wins. Owners must have write access. It is only a requirement if the ruleset says "require review from code owners".

    Keep dependencies current

    One required check for a merge queue

    Who reviews the pipeline

    Sources. Dependabot options reference, Managing a merge queue, About code owners

    What you just learned

    • Require one gate job, not a list of job names, and make it listen to merge_group.
    • Dependabot, rulesets and CODEOWNERS are the files and settings around the workflow, and they matter as much.
    • A gate job needs if: always(), or a failure upstream skips it, and a skip counts as success.
    14

    Commands you should know by heart

    Goal: start, watch, debug and re-run a pipeline, manage its secrets, and look up a commit SHA, all from the terminal and without a search engine.

    Why this step

    The pipeline runs in the cloud, but you work on it from a terminal. The same twenty commands cover almost every day: they save you opening the browser to find a run, and they are the glue in scripts. Each drill takes a plain-English request, and checks what you type against the real command, including every flag it accepts.

    Start, watch and debug a run

    Sources. GitHub CLI manual, Manually running a workflow

    What you just learned

    • gh run list | watch | view --log-failed | rerun --failed is the debugging loop.
    • Put secrets in with gh secret set NAME and let it ask for the value.
    • gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/commits/TAG --jq .sha turns a tag into the SHA to pin.
    15

    Delivery patterns: several workflows, three environments, real apps

    Goal: know how a team's pipeline is split into files, how settings and passwords reach a job, how one build travels from dev to uat to prod, and what is different about deploying a .NET API and a single-page app.

    Why this step

    So far every lab was one file with one purpose. A real repository has several workflow files that share work, and the same build must run in three places with three sets of settings. Nothing here is new syntax. It is how the pieces you know are arranged, and where the settings come from. You read this step, then write all of it yourself in the next one.

    1. One file per purpose

    A workflow file answers two questions: when does it run, and what is it allowed to do. When two things have different answers, they belong in different files.

    FileStarts onDoesMay use
    pr.ymlpull_requestBuilds and tests. Deploys nothingNo secrets, no environment, a read-only token
    release.ymlpush to mainBuilds once, then dev, uat, prodEnvironments, their secrets, cloud login
    build.ymlworkflow_callThe build itself, written once and called by the two aboveWhatever the caller allows
    deploy.ymlworkflow_callDeploys to the one environment it is toldThat environment's variables and secrets
    • A pull request workflow that cannot deploy. If pr.yml names no secret and no environment, no change to it by a contributor can reach production. A pull request from a fork gets no secrets and a read-only token in any case, so a build that needs neither works for everyone.
    • The build is written once. The pull request check and the release call the same reusable build.yml, so what you tested is what you ship.
    • A called workflow is part of the caller's run. Its artifacts can be downloaded by the caller's later jobs, and its outputs are read with needs.<job>.outputs.
    • A job that calls a workflow has no runs-on, no steps and no environment. It has uses, with, secrets and needs.

    The other way to chain: workflow_run. It starts a workflow when another one is requested or completes. Use it only when the second workflow needs secrets that the first must not see, for example to comment on a pull request from a fork. It runs the file from the default branch, with secrets, and chains at most three levels deep. For "build, then deploy", a reusable workflow is simpler and shows as one run.

    2. How a value gets into a job

    Kind of valueWhere you keep itHow the workflow reads itShown in logs
    The same everywhere, safe to read (Release)In the file: env: on the workflow, a job or a step$NAME in a script, env.NAME in an expressionYes
    Differs per environment, not secret (a URL, a namespace)A variable: Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions${{ vars.NAME }}Yes
    Grants access (a password, a token)A secret, in the same place${{ secrets.NAME }}Masked as ***
    Worked out during the run (a version, an image tag)Nowhere: a step writes itecho "NAME=value" >> "$GITHUB_ENV" for later steps, >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT" for other steps and jobsYes
    • The most specific wins. For variables and secrets: environment over repository over organization. For env:: step over job over workflow.
    • Environment values need the environment. A job sees an environment's variables and secrets only when it has environment: that-name, and its secrets only after any required reviewer has approved.
    • A wrong name is silent. A secret or variable that does not exist gives an empty text and no error. This is the most common reason for "it works in dev and not in uat".
    • Keep a secret narrow. Put it in the env of the one step that needs it. At job or workflow level it is handed to every step, including actions written by other people. Never write ${{ secrets.X }} inside a script.
    • $GITHUB_ENV starts at the next step. The step that writes a value cannot read it yet.
    • Not in if. secrets cannot be read in an if:. Put it in env and test the variable.
    • A reusable workflow gets no secrets by itself. The caller passes them, one by one or all with secrets: inherit.

    3. Dev, uat, prod: build once, deploy three times

    The rule is short: the thing that reaches production is the same thing that was tested. So the image or the publish folder is built in one job, and three deploy jobs take it to three places. What differs between the places is not in the YAML. It is in the three environments in the repository's settings.

    EnvironmentVariable K8S_NAMESPACESecret DB_PASSWORDProtection
    devtodo-devthe dev passwordNone: every merge deploys
    uattodo-uatthe uat passwordA tester approves
    prodtodo-prodthe prod passwordA reviewer approves, and only main may deploy
    • List build in every stage's needs. A job can read the outputs of the jobs in its own needs list only. Through dev alone, needs.build.outputs.image_tag is empty.
    • One deployment per environment at a time: concurrency with the environment in the group name and cancel-in-progress: false.
    • The job's name is a label. Where it deploys is decided by the value of environment. Copying a stage and forgetting that one word is the classic mistake (scenario 12 in step 18).

    You can run all of this without a cluster. Make the three environments, give each a different variable, and let the deploy script print what it would do:

    Plans. Environments, their secrets and their protection rules work in public repositories on every plan. In a private repository they need GitHub Pro, Team or Enterprise, and required reviewers need Enterprise. Practise in the public repository from step 20.

    4. A .NET API: overwriting appsettings

    ASP.NET Core reads its settings from several places, one after the other, and a later place wins for any setting it also has:

    OrderSourceWhat the pipeline does with it
    1appsettings.jsonNothing. It is in the repository, with the defaults
    2appsettings.<Environment>.jsonWrites it at deploy time, for settings that are not secret
    3Environment variablesSets them where the app runs, for secrets
    4Command-line argumentsRarely used
    • <Environment> is the value of ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT where the app runs. When it is not set, the app uses Production.
    • The capital letters must match on Linux. With ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=uat, the file appsettings.Uat.json is skipped, and a missing settings file is not an error.
    • In a variable name, __ is the : between levels. The setting ConnectionStrings:Todos is overridden by the variable ConnectionStrings__Todos. One underscore does nothing.
    • An override needs the same shape. To replace Api:BaseUrl, the file must contain {"Api": {"BaseUrl": …}}. Anything else is a new setting that nobody reads.
    • Write JSON with jq, never with echo or sed. jq -n --arg quotes every value correctly. It is already on GitHub's runners.

    These are not claims from memory. This is a real .NET 10 app on Linux, with Api:BaseUrl and ConnectionStrings:Todos in appsettings.json and an appsettings.Uat.json beside it, started six ways:

    Started withThe app's environmentApi:BaseUrl came fromConnectionStrings:Todos came from
    Nothing setProductionappsettings.Production.jsonappsettings.json
    ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=UatUatappsettings.Uat.jsonappsettings.json
    ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=uatuatappsettings.json: the Uat file was skippedappsettings.json
    Uat and ConnectionStrings__Todos=…Uatappsettings.Uat.jsonthe variable
    Uat and ConnectionStrings_Todos=…Uatappsettings.Uat.jsonappsettings.json: one underscore was ignored
    Uat, Api__BaseUrl=… and --Api:BaseUrl=…Uatthe command lineappsettings.json

    5. An Angular app, or any single-page app

    The output of ng build is a folder of static files. Deploying it means copying that folder to something that serves files: a bucket behind a CDN, GitHub Pages, or nginx in a container. Three things need care, and they are the same for React and Vue.

    ProblemWhyWhat the pipeline does
    Settings are compiled inAngular's environment.ts and --configuration are applied while building. A build made for dev points at dev for everBuilds once. At deploy time it writes a small config.json next to index.html, and the app fetches it when it starts
    Browsers keep filesA production build puts a hash in the name of each script and stylesheet (main-5T3KQ2AB.js), so those never change. index.html keeps its name and names the current scriptsUploads *.js and *.css with a one-year cache, and everything else with no-cache
    A release is not instantFor a moment the server has a mix of old and new files, and open tabs still hold the old index.htmlUploads the hashed files first and index.html last, and leaves the old hashed files in place
    • Everything in config.json is public. A browser app cannot keep a secret: anything it can read, its users can read. Passwords and keys stay on the API.
    • The filters are read left to right and the last match wins. --exclude "*" --include "*.js" means nothing, except scripts. With --delete, files that a filter excludes are left alone in the bucket, which is how the old scripts survive.
    • no-cache does not mean "do not store". It means "ask the server whether it changed before using your copy". That is one tiny request, and a new release is seen at once.
    • A cached index.html cannot be fixed from the server. If it ever went out with a one-year cache, the browsers that have it will not ask again (scenario 14 in step 18).
    • Routes need a fallback. For /todos/42 the server has no file, so it must answer with index.html and let the app's router take over. On CloudFront that is a custom error response, on nginx try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;.
    • A sub-path needs a base href. If the app is served from /todo/ and not from /, build with ng build --base-href /todo/.

    The same app on GitHub Pages needs no cloud account, which makes it a good way to practise. Pages takes one artifact and publishes it. Choose GitHub Actions as the source under Settings → Pages first.

    What you just learned

    • One workflow file per trigger and purpose. The pull request file builds and cannot deploy. The build is one reusable file.
    • Fixed values in env, per-environment settings in vars, anything that grants access in secrets, and a secret only in the step that needs it.
    • Build once, deploy three times. The environments hold the differences, and the YAML stays the same.
    • .NET: a later source wins, __ is the separator, and the environment name must match the file name exactly.
    • A single-page app: settings from a file fetched at start-up, long cache only for hashed files, hashed files first and index.html last.
    16

    Write it from scratch

    Goal: write twelve pipelines from an empty editor, from a ten-line greeting to three environments and a single-page app, using only a checklist.

    Why this step

    In the guided labs the editor could start you off. Here it always starts empty, and the right-hand list says what to build and not how. The lab shows an error the moment you type one. When something is not met yet it stays grey. Use hints only when you are stuck for more than a minute: the point is to get the syntax into your fingers.

    The challenges get harder one by one. Your work is saved in this browser, so you can leave and come back. Challenges 6 and 10 have several files: each file is a tab above the editor, and the checklist says which file a requirement is about. The keys that fit on the current line are listed under the editor, Next line shows only the next line you need, and Show solution opens the finished file without touching yours.

    What you just learned

    • You can write a workflow's skeleton, its triggers, a matrix, a cache, an image build and a staged deploy without a template.
    • The same few patterns come back: a condition used twice, a gate job, one job's permission raised.
    • You can split a pipeline into files, pass variables and secrets the right way, and take one build through dev, uat and prod, for a .NET API and for a single-page app.
    17

    The capstone: the enterprise pipeline

    Goal: write one pipeline for the Todo project that a security review would pass: 20 requirements, from an empty editor.

    Why this step

    This is the whole job in one file: continuous integration on pull requests and the merge queue, a signed and attested image for each push and release tag, a staged deployment with approval, no stored cloud keys, and every action pinned. If you can write this without looking, you can write the pipeline of a real team.

    Build it in layers and check the preview after each: 1. triggers, permissions, concurrency. 2. api and ui. 3. dependency-review. 4. image, with sign and attest. 5. staging and production. 6. the ci-ok gate. One trap is waiting: a job can read needs.X.outputs only for jobs in its own needs, not for jobs further up the chain.

    What you just learned

    • You can design the whole graph: CI jobs, an image job, two gated deploys, and a gate for the ruleset.
    • The settings that complete it are outside the file: the ruleset, the environment rules, the cloud trust policies and Dependabot.
    18

    Read it and fix it

    Goal: given a broken pipeline and what the team saw, find the cause and fix it, from a one-word typo to a pipeline with seven separate faults.

    Why this step

    Most of your life with pipelines is reading ones you did not write, at the moment something has gone wrong. That is a different skill from writing. Each scenario starts with the symptom: a message, a log line, a person's complaint. You read the file, form a theory, and fix it. The right-hand list shows only how many problems remain, until you fix each one.

    A method for reading a pipeline

    1. Does it start? Triggers and filters. Branch or tag? Which files? Is it on the default branch (for schedule and workflow_dispatch)? Use the preview.
    2. What may it do? permissions at the top and on each job. Anything broader than the job needs is a finding.
    3. In what order? needs, if and the status functions. Which jobs run, which are skipped, and why?
    4. Where does text go? Every ${{ }} inside run: is the value written by someone outside the team? Is a secret pasted into a script?
    5. What does it depend on? Every uses: a branch, a tag, or a SHA? An old major version?
    6. What can run away? timeout-minutes, concurrency, caches that never hit, artifacts that collide.
    7. What changes production? Environments, approval, concurrency on deploys, image tags.

    The first eleven are in order of difficulty. The last three are delivery problems from step 15: the wrong environment, .NET settings that are ignored, and a web app that stays old. Each is a real mistake that people make.

    What you just learned

    • Start from the symptom, then read in a fixed order: start, permissions, order, text, dependencies, limits, production.
    • A skipped job is quiet, a missing permission is loud, and an injected script is invisible until someone uses it.
    19

    Sandbox: check your own workflow

    Goal: paste any workflow from your own repositories and see what the checker and the run preview say.

    The editor below starts with a small example. Replace it with a file of your own. The checker is the same one used in every lab, and the preview shows which jobs would start for each event. Nothing leaves your browser.

    Run it for real on GitHub

    Goal: take any exercise from this page, run it on GitHub, watch it, and read its logs, from the terminal.

    Why this step

    The lab checks what you write, but it cannot run it. Only a real run shows you a runner starting, a cache hit, a job waiting for approval, a login that works. You need a repository to push to, and a few commands, most of which you already practised in step 14.

    1. Pick where to practise

    A throwaway public repositoryYour private infra-setup
    CostFree: standard GitHub-hosted runners cost nothing in public repositoriesUses your plan's free minutes (2,000 a month on GitHub Free), then is billed
    Code to buildNone until you add someThe real API and UI are already at src/api and src/ui
    CodeQL, dependency reviewWorkNeed GitHub Advanced Security
    Environments with their own variables and secretsWorkNeed GitHub Pro, Team or Enterprise
    Environment reviewers and wait timersWorkNot on Free, Pro or Team
    Artifact attestationsWorkNeed GitHub Enterprise Cloud
    RiskNone: nothing real is deployedA publish lab really pushes an image, a deploy lab really deploys

    Use the public practice repository for learning, and move a workflow into infra-setup when you want it for real. Do not put secrets you care about in a public repository's workflows.

    2. Put an exercise in, push, watch

    Use the Copy button of a lab and paste into a file in .github/workflows/. The folder must be at the root of the repository, and the file must end in .yml or .yaml. Lint it, push, then follow the run:

    3. Make the right event happen

    The workflow listens forHow to trigger it
    pushgit push to a branch the filters match
    pull_requestPush a branch, then gh pr create --fill. Every later push to that branch runs it again
    workflow_dispatchgh workflow run file.yml --ref main -f name=value. The file must be on the default branch first
    a tag (tags: ['v*'])git tag v1.2.0 && git push origin v1.2.0
    scheduleWait for the time, or add workflow_dispatch beside it and start it by hand. It only runs from the default branch
    merge_groupTurn on a merge queue in a ruleset for main, then choose "Merge when ready" on a pull request

    4. What each lab needs before it can pass on GitHub

    LabsSet up first
    1, 3, 4, 9 (structure), 18 and the gate jobsNothing. They only use echo
    2, 5, 14 and "from scratch" 2A .NET project in src/api (the dotnet new line above, or your real API)
    6 and "from scratch" 4The Angular app in src/ui with its package-lock.json. Use infra-setup, or copy the folder
    7gh secret set NOTIFY_API_KEY and gh variable set NOTIFY_URL --body <address>; the comment step needs a pull request
    8, 16 and "from scratch" 5A Docker Hub access token: gh variable set DOCKERHUB_USERNAME --body <you> and gh secret set DOCKERHUB_TOKEN. A Dockerfile in src/api
    9 (for the gate to hold)The environments staging and production, with you as a required reviewer on production (Settings → Environments)
    10 and "from scratch" 9An AWS account with GitHub as an OIDC provider and a role whose trust policy matches your repository's sub. Without it the login step fails, which is the expected result
    11 and 12Both files in the repository: the caller needs .github/workflows/build-image.yml to exist
    "From scratch" 3The .NET project, the Angular app and a Dockerfile in src/api. No secrets and no settings: that is its point
    "From scratch" 6 and 10Every tab saved as its own file in .github/workflows/, with the name on the tab. For 6, 7 and 10: the environments, variables and secrets from step 15 (the loop that creates dev, uat and prod), and a scripts/deploy.sh or scripts/migrate.sh that is executable and only prints what it would do
    "From scratch" 11The variables ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT, API_BASE_URL and LOG_LEVEL and the secret DB_CONNECTION_STRING on each environment. Without a cluster the kubectl apply step fails, which is the expected result: the settings file is written before it
    "From scratch" 12An AWS account with a bucket, a CloudFront distribution and an OIDC role. Without one, use the GitHub Pages workflow from step 15, which needs nothing but the repository
    13Save it as .github/actions/setup-todo-api/action.yml and use it from a workflow after a checkout step
    15A public repository (or GitHub Advanced Security), with the dependency graph enabled
    17 and 19Save as .github/dependabot.yml and .github/CODEOWNERS. The CODEOWNERS teams must exist and have write access

    gh api fills in {owner} and {repo} from the repository you are in. Required reviewers are added in Settings → Environments.

    5. Read what happened

    • The run page (the Actions tab, or gh run view --web) shows the job graph you saw in the preview, with real timings.
    • A skipped job is grey. Compare it with what the lab's preview said for that event.
    • A waiting job with an environment shows "Waiting for review". Approve it there, or with the review button.
    • Debug logging: gh run rerun <id> --debug runs it again with step debug logs.
    • The cache: the second run of a cached job prints "Cache restored". gh cache list shows what is stored.

    6. Clean up

    Before you push a workflow to infra-setup. A workflow starts running the moment it reaches GitHub and its trigger matches. A file with on: push runs on that very push. Read its triggers, its permissions and what it publishes or deploys first, exactly as in step 18.

    Sources. GitHub Actions billing, Manually running a workflow, Enabling debug logging, Managing environments

    What you just learned

    • The loop is: lint, push, gh run watch, gh run view --log-failed.
    • Each trigger has its own way to fire, and manual and scheduled workflows must be on the default branch.
    • A public practice repository is free and has every feature; a private one needs the right plan for some of them.

    When something breaks

    What you seeLikely causeWhat to do
    The Actions tab shows Invalid workflow file, and no run startsA YAML or structure error in the fileRun actionlint locally, or paste the file in the sandbox (step 19)
    You pushed and nothing ranA branch, tag or path filter does not match; the file is not on the default branch (for schedule and workflow_dispatch); the commit message has [skip ci] (or [ci skip], [no ci], [skip actions], [actions skip])Use the run preview with the same event, and read the filters
    A required check stays Pending foreverThe workflow was skipped by a path filter, a branch filter or a commit message, so its check never reportedDo not filter a required workflow. Require one gate job instead (step 13)
    A job shows This check was skippedIts if was false, or a job it needs failed or was skippedRead the if. Check github.ref vs github.ref_name, and look for text around ${{ }}
    Resource not accessible by integration (HTTP 403)The GITHUB_TOKEN lacks a permission for that callAdd the scope to the job's permissions (and only that job)
    The cache is never restoredThe key changes every run (for example it contains github.sha), or the cache was created on a branch the run cannot readKey on hashFiles of the input files; add restore-keys
    An artifact upload fails with (409) Conflict: an artifact with this name already existsTwo jobs, often matrix legs, upload the same namePut the matrix values in the name; download with pattern and merge-multiple
    The cloud says Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentityThe token's sub (or aud) does not match the role's trust policy: wrong environment, wrong repository, or old vs new subject formatPrint the claims with github/actions-oidc-debugger; compare with the trust policy; check the job declares the environment
    A run was cancelled and nobody cancelled itcancel-in-progress: true in a concurrency group, or the job reached its timeout-minutesCheck concurrency and timeouts; never cancel deploys
    A scheduled workflow stopped runningIn a public repository, schedules are disabled after 60 days without repository activitygh workflow enable <file>
    A variable or secret is empty in one environment and fine in anotherIt is not set for that environment, its name is spelled differently there, or the job does not name the environment. A missing name gives an empty text and no errorgh variable list --env uat and gh secret list --env uat; check the job's environment; in a called workflow, check the caller passes secrets: inherit (step 15)
    A .NET app ignores appsettings.Uat.json or a setting from an environment variableThe environment name does not match the file name letter for letter, the override has another shape than the setting, or the variable has one underscore where it needs twoRead the app's start-up log line Hosting environment (step 18, scenario 13)
    Users still see the old web app after a releaseindex.html was uploaded with a long cache, so browsers do not ask againLong cache only for files with a hash in their name; no-cache for index.html (step 18, scenario 14)
    Secrets are empty in a run for a pull request from a forkFork pull requests get a read-only token and no secrets, by designDo not work around it with pull_request_target (step 18, scenario 10)
    An environment has required reviewers set but the job does not waitYour plan does not support them for this repository (private repositories need a higher plan)Check Settings → Environments for a warning, and the plan notes in step 9
    The lab says the checker is unavailableThe browser lacks WebAssembly or DecompressionStreamUse a current Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari. The YAML and requirement checks still work
    →

    Where to go next

    You can write and read a pipeline. These widen what you can run it on and how you run it at scale:

    • Wire it to the cluster. Part 1 of the Todo series commits the new image tag to values.yaml and lets Argo CD deploy it. Replace that script with the image job from the capstone, and let the deploy jobs update the chart instead of calling kubectl.
    • Your own runners. Self-hosted runners and the Actions Runner Controller on Kubernetes give you your own hardware and network access, and need more care: they are not isolated between runs, so never use them for untrusted pull requests.
    • Larger and slim runners. GitHub-hosted larger runners (Team and Enterprise plans) have more CPU and static IP addresses. ubuntu-slim is a single-CPU, lower-cost runner for light jobs, with a 15-minute job limit.
    • Share across an organisation. Workflow templates in the organisation's .github repository, and reusable workflows called by tag, give every team the same pipeline.
    • Lock the dependencies. When workflow dependency lockfiles reach your plan, gh actions-lock pins every action, transitive ones included.
    • More clouds. The OIDC pattern is the same for Azure, Google Cloud, HashiCorp Vault and others: only the trust configuration and the login action change.
    • Custom protection rules. Environments can ask an outside system (an observability or change-management tool) to approve a deployment, through GitHub Apps.
    • Terraform in the pipeline. Part 6 builds the layers. A pipeline job can run terraform plan on every pull request and apply after approval, with OIDC to the cloud.
    Written October 2026 against the GitHub Actions documentation and the action repositories as published that month (actions/checkout 7, setup-dotnet 6, setup-node 7, cache 6, upload-artifact 7, download-artifact 8, docker actions 4 to 7, cosign-installer 4.1, attest 4, codeql-action 4, configure-aws-credentials 6) and actionlint 1.7.12. GitHub changes this area often: the lab reads each action's own repository for versions, so re-run the build script to refresh them.
